subject: Interconnect options for private deployment: AuroraHealth
messages:
From: Samira Khan <samira.k@aurorahealth.com>
To: Priya Natarajan <priya@redwood.ai>
Cc: Alex Ruiz <alex.ruiz@aurorahealth.com>
Date: 2027-04-27T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Interconnect for Redwood Private deployment

Hi Priya,

Thanks for the walkthrough yesterday. We're preparing to move a subset of Aurora Health's inference workloads onto Redwood Private in us-west-2 and need help deciding the right network model for the control-plane <-> customer VPC connectivity. Our constraints:

- Sensitive PHI in-scope (SOC2/HIPAA constraints).
- Expected steady egress for production: ~120Mbps sustained, with occasional spikes to 400Mbps.
- Multi-account setup: we operate separate accounts for prod/stage.
- We want minimal blast radius and clear auditing for access.

Can you outline the tradeoffs between VPC Peering, AWS PrivateLink (VPC Endpoint Services), and site-to-site VPN for this use case? Specifically:
- Operational complexity and who manages routes/ENIs
- Support for cross-account access and least-privilege patterns
- Typical latency/throughput expectations and failure modes
- Cost hotspots we should budget for (data egress, endpoints, transit GW)
- Any compliance implications (auditability, key separation)

I attached a brief network inventory for Aurora (subnets/CIDRs/peering/transit) — "aurora-network-inventory.pdf".

Would appreciate a short recommendation and a suggested pilot plan (what you recommend we test first).

Best,
Samira
---
Samira Khan
Director, Cloud Infrastructure
Aurora Health

Thanks Samira — this is a great summary and the inventory helps. Looping in Marcus (network architect) and Karthik (product/ops) to provide an architect-level comparison and a short pilot plan.

Initial asks from our side to make the recommendation tighter:
- Confirm whether you require cross-region failover or everything stays in us-west-2 for now.
- Any approved CIDR ranges we must avoid (we saw 10.0.0.0/8 used widely in your estate).
- Will you accept a managed endpoint (PrivateLink) that creates an ENI in your subnet, or do you need zero-ENI footprint?

We'll come back with an option matrix and a recommended pilot approach (likely 2-week pilot + observability checks). I've attached our Redwood Private checklist for quick alignment — "redwood-private-deploy-checklist.md".

Thanks,

From: Marcus Lin <marcus.lin@redwood.ai>
To: Priya Natarajan <priya@redwood.ai>, Samira Khan <samira.k@aurorahealth.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>
Date: 2027-04-28T10:30:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Interconnect for Redwood Private deployment

Hi all — I reviewed the inventory and the constraints. Below is a practical comparison and the recommendation I would land on for Aurora's profile.

Quick TL;DR recommendation:
- Pilot: AWS PrivateLink (VPC Endpoint Service) in us-west-2 for control-plane traffic and metadata APIs.
- If you need very high sustained throughput between model-serving nodes inside your VPC and Redwood-managed GPUs in the same account/region, consider a dedicated VPC Peering/Transit Gateway path separate from the control plane.
- Site-to-Site VPN: fallback for on-prem/hybrid or if you require encrypted tunnel over public internet to a specific on-prem datacenter.

Detailed tradeoffs:
1) VPC Peering
- Pros: Low latency, high throughput (no NAT bottleneck), simple L3 routing for same-region, good for intra-account or trusted accounts.
- Cons: Not transitive (cannot route through peering to other VPCs), cross-account requires explicit peering from both sides, careful CIDR planning required (no overlapping CIDRs).
- Ops: You (Aurora) manage route tables; Redwood would have to peer into your account (or you into ours) and manage peer attachments.
- Compliance: Works fine but increases attack surface if many peering links exist.

2) AWS PrivateLink (Endpoint Service)
- Pros: Cross-account friendly, minimal routing changes on customer side (creates an ENI in a designated subnet), isolates the service behind an endpoint, supports security policies at the endpoint level, easier to audit via VPC Flow Logs and endpoint policies.
- Cons: Per-GB endpoint charges and ENI costs; endpoints have bandwidth soft-limits depending on instance types backing the service, but for control-plane RPCs and model control traffic it's usually fine.
- Ops: Redwood runs the service; Aurora grants permission to create/accept endpoints. Least-privilege pattern is straightforward and blast radius is small.
- Compliance: Better for auditability and separation of responsibilities — good for PHI when combined with KMS separation for application-level data.

3) Site-to-Site VPN
- Pros: Works for on-prem or when private networking across providers is required; supports IPsec encryption and can be monitored.
- Cons: Higher latency, lower sustained throughput compared to peering or PrivateLink; operational overhead for tunnels and BGP.
- Ops: Aurora or your network team manages VPN endpoints; Redwood can provide routing/peer configuration but won't manage customer VPN appliances.
- Compliance: Acceptable but you must validate key rotation and logging for IPsec endpoints.

Other considerations:
- Transit Gateway: If you plan multiple VPCs or many accounts, a Transit Gateway (TGW) in Aurora’s account simplifies routing and centralizes egress policies. TGW + TGW attachments + PrivateLink can be a stable pattern (PrivateLink for control-plane; TGW for bulk east-west traffic).
- Monitoring & Observability: VPC Flow Logs + endpoint logs + Redwood's token-level tracing should be enabled for the pilot.
- Failure modes: PrivateLink: endpoint ENI failure -> failover to another AZ or endpoint instance; Peering: route table misconfig leads to blackholing; VPN: tunnel flaps -> graceful degrade.
- Cost hotspots: endpoint-hour + per-GB endpoint data, Transit Gateway hourly + data, cross-AZ data charges if endpoints span AZs.

Suggested pilot plan (2 weeks):
1) PrivateLink pilot (control-plane only) in a single prod-test VPC in us-west-2:
   - Aurora creates an endpoint in a dedicated subnet and allows Redwood's service ID.
   - Smoke tests: control-plane API calls, auth/audit logs, token/role exchange, small model run (1-2 pods) for end-to-end.
   - Observability: enable VPC Flow Logs, Redwood's request tracing, and a baseline of latency/p50/p95.
2) If you need higher data plane throughput between your model-serving nodes and Redwood (rare for our managed offering) schedule additional peering/TGW evaluation.

Attachments: design sketch and option cost notes -> "interconnect-options-arc.pdf" (high level diagram + rough cost calc).

Happy to run a short call to walk through the pilot steps and get the endpoint creation window scheduled.

--
Marcus Lin
Senior Network Architect, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Interconnect for Redwood Private deployment

Thanks Marcus and team — this is exactly the clarity we needed. A few follow-ups:

- We accept the PrivateLink pilot for control-plane in us-west-2. Please provide the Service Name and the exact permission policy we should apply so our infra team can pre-approve it.
- We will stand up the endpoint in a dedicated subnet (non-overlapping CIDR) and enable VPC Flow Logs for the pilot window.
- Can Redwood provide a short test plan for the smoke tests you listed and a one-week timeline to get everything instrumented? Ideally we run the pilot for 10 business days and then decide on peering/TGW for the data-plane if needed.
- Please also share a SOC2 artifact link we can include in our compliance package (we referenced "SOC2_report_redwood_2026.pdf" in our internal request).

Next steps I propose:
- Redwood sends: Service Name + endpoint permission JSON + smoke test playbook + pilot schedule (proposed start next Tue).
- Aurora: create endpoint and share the endpoint-id, we will open a narrow maintenance window for acceptance testing.

Appreciate the quick turnaround.

Regards,
Samira
